name: The World of AI: AI Courses directory, a curated catalogue of 13 courses
title: The World of AI: AI Courses directory, a curated catalogue of 13 courses
answer: This is a catalogue page from The World of AI listing AI courses, 13 in total with 11 free, each curated by level and audience with one verified source and re-verified daily. Its most useful point for education readers is the split it draws between university graduate courses, which it describes as structured around exam driven theory, and industry courses, which it describes as code first or hands on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its research and learning section, inside a larger site it describes as an atlas of artificial intelligence built from one database covering state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests. The page is a catalogue of AI courses, each entry carrying a level, an intended audience, a cost note and a verification date. It states a last verified date of 2026-09-28 and says source links are re-verified daily. It also states that membership is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship, and that nothing listed is paid placement. The page supplies a citation line for itself and carries promotional material for books by Stephen R. Jordan and for SRJ Consulting and Services.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists courses with level, intended audience, cost and verification date. DeepLearning.AI appears on Coursera at beginner level for managers, executives and anyone working alongside technical teams, free to audit with a certificate fee listed on the page, and again at intermediate level for people who have finished the ML Specialization. Dataquest is listed as beginner level for developers who want hands on practice with LLM APIs, on a subscription. fast.ai is beginner to intermediate for programmers and top down learners, free, with companion code. A DeepLearning.AI and Stanford course on Coursera is beginner level and described as the first course for most people, free to audit with a paid certificate. The page says four of the tracked courses are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. It argues this split matters because university courses are generally structured around exam driven theory while the industry courses are described as code first or hands on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. Three courses list a public companion code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page states 13 AI courses, 11 of them free and 3 with public companion code, each with one verified source, re-verified daily, with a last verified date of 2026-09-28. It names four university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, and three courses with public code repositories, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. It also says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, a count that does not match the 13 stated at the top. It states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in education can use this page as a dated, sourced list of the courses and credentials the field currently points to, which is what the industry page cites it for. The level, audience and cost fields, and the distinction between university theory courses and industry code first courses, are the parts most likely to be useful when advising learners or mapping training to skills, since the page says the skills these teach map to the AI Skills Graph. It is a catalogue rather than evidence about learning outcomes, so it supports questions about what exists and what it costs, not about what works.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: This is a directory page, not a study. It gives no enrollment, completion, outcome or quality data, and no method beyond a statement that membership is editorial and based on significance rather than sponsorship. The course entries are short, with no syllabi or assessment detail. The page contradicts itself on how many courses it tracks, saying 13 at the top and ten in the body. It also carries promotional material for books by Stephen R. Jordan and for SRJ Consulting and Services, including a novel and a list of audit products, which sits alongside the course list. The content is dated 2026-09-28 and described as re-verified daily.
